original_question: Can one give an explicit fast growing sequence of positive integers, meaning a(n) grows faster than every power of n, that is good for multiple recurrence and multiple convergence both for powers of a single transformation and for commuting transformations?
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s actual target: it asks for an explicit fast-growing sequence of positive integers and correctly requires both multiple recurrence and multiple convergence, for powers of a single transformation and for commuting transformations. That is exactly the scope of Section 4.6, Problem 8. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
missing_details: The paper gives an exact definition of "fast growing": a(n) must satisfy lim_{n→∞} (log a(n) / log n) = ∞, equivalently a(n) = n^{b(n)} with b(n) → ∞.
"Multiple" means "for every ℓ ∈ N"; your draft does not state this quantifier.

For recurrence of powers, the formal meaning is: for every ℓ, every nonzero integers k1,...,kℓ, every invertible measure-preserving system (X, 𝓧, μ, T), and every A ∈ 𝓧 with μ(A) > 0, there exists n such that μ(A ∩ T^{-k1 a(n)}A ∩ ... ∩ T^{-kℓ a(n)}A) > 0.

For recurrence of commuting transformations, the formal meaning is: for every ℓ, every probability space (X, 𝓧, μ), every commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T1,...,Tℓ, and every A ∈ 𝓧 with μ(A) > 0, there exists n such that μ(A ∩ T1^{-a(n)}A ∩ ... ∩ Tℓ^{-a(n)}A) > 0.

For convergence of powers, the paper means Cesàro mean convergence in L^2(μ) of the averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T^{k1 a(n)}f1 ... T^{kℓ a(n)}fℓ for every ℓ, every integers k1,...,kℓ, every invertible measure-preserving system, and every f1,...,fℓ ∈ L∞(μ).

For convergence of commuting transformations, the paper means Cesàro mean convergence in L^2(μ) of the averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T1^{a(n)}f1 ... Tℓ^{a(n)}fℓ for every ℓ, every probability space, every commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T1,...,Tℓ, and every f1,...,fℓ ∈ L∞(μ).

The ambient setting is ergodic-theoretic, not algebraic: no ring/field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency hypotheses are part of this problem; the relevant hidden assumptions are positivity of the sequence, invertibility of the transformations, commutativity in the commuting case, and mean convergence rather than pointwise convergence.

To be fully paper-faithful, the question should ask for one explicit sequence satisfying all four properties simultaneously: multiple recurrence of powers, multiple convergence of powers, multiple recurrence of commuting transformations, and multiple convergence of commuting transformations.
refined_question: Give an explicit sequence a: N → N with lim_{n→∞} (log a(n) / log n) = ∞ such that a(n) is simultaneously good for multiple recurrence of powers, good for multiple convergence of powers, good for multiple recurrence of commuting transformations, and good for multiple convergence of commuting transformations; that is: (i) for every ℓ ∈ N, every nonzero integers k1,...,kℓ, every invertible measure-preserving system (X, 𝓧, μ, T), and every A ∈ 𝓧 with μ(A) > 0, there exists n ∈ N with μ(A ∩ T^{-k1 a(n)}A ∩ ... ∩ T^{-kℓ a(n)}A) > 0; (ii) for every ℓ ∈ N, every integers k1,...,kℓ, every invertible measure-preserving system (X, 𝓧, μ, T), and every f1,...,fℓ ∈ L∞(μ), the Cesàro averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T^{k1 a(n)}f1 ... T^{kℓ a(n)}fℓ converge in L^2(μ); (iii) for every ℓ ∈ N, every probability space (X, 𝓧, μ), every commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T1,...,Tℓ, and every A ∈ 𝓧 with μ(A) > 0, there exists n ∈ N with μ(A ∩ T1^{-a(n)}A ∩ ... ∩ Tℓ^{-a(n)}A) > 0; and (iv) for every ℓ ∈ N, every such T1,...,Tℓ, and every f1,...,fℓ ∈ L∞(μ), the averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N T1^{a(n)}f1 ... Tℓ^{a(n)}fℓ converge in L^2(μ).
justification: The draft clearly targets the fast-growing-sequence problem in Section 4.6: the paper first defines "fast growing" and then asks for an explicit example that is good for multiple recurrence and convergence for both powers and commuting transformations. To make the question genuinely stand-alone, one has to unpack the paper’s shorthand "good for multiple recurrence/convergence of powers/commuting transformations" using the formal sequence-level definitions in Section 3.1, Definition 3.2, and Section 3.2, Definition 3.4, together with the underlying collection-level definitions in Definitions 3.1 and 3.3. Those definitions supply the missing quantifiers over ℓ, the roles of the integers k1,...,kℓ, the requirement that the transformations be invertible and commuting in the commuting case, the positive-measure recurrence condition, and the fact that convergence means Cesàro convergence in the mean (L^2), not pointwise convergence. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.3808))
